item.title: Did 41 Years of Therapy Actually Help Me?
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Did 41 Years of Therapy Actually Help Me?

Personal Perspective: Looking for answers didn't keep me stuck—it set me free.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Seeking therapy isn't weakness. It can be a determined search for answers and healing.
  • Therapy maintained mental stability and enabled hard life choices, not dependency.
  • Long-term therapy can shift from crisis survival to wellness maintenance over time.
Source: Jon Tyson/Unsplash

It started when I was young. Pretty young, anyway—18 years old. I didn’t know it would continue until I was well into my 50s; 59, to be exact. But I have cut down. I don’t do it weekly anymore, or biweekly or even monthly.

Not that there’s anything wrong with that. Sometimes it’s necessary, right? It’s a coping mechanism. There’s a time and place for everything.

Over the past 41 years I have seen:

  • Three registered clinical counsellors.
  • One campus counsellor.
  • Two social workers.
  • One sex therapist (yes, really).
  • Seven psychiatrists.

That's 14 in total. Two more and I get a free appointment.

I don’t say shrink. One of my favourite psychiatrists—yes, it’s possible to have a good psychiatrist who becomes your favourite—heard me say shrink once, and he looked so hurt. He’s dead now, but I want to honour his memory.

You might be thinking: God, 41 years of therapy. Who needs that much help? I certainly don’t.

Really? Really? Are ya sure?

Think of all the counsellors I’ve seen like all the things you’ve tried over the years, hoping to find the one that works: exercise programs, diets, fishing flies you’ve put on your rod, lipstick shades, productivity apps, aftershaves, perfumes—you get the idea.

In reality, it's more like how you might feel if you were diagnosed with a mysterious illness, or your partner was, or God forbid, your child. You'd likely seek out every solution, talk to every doctor, research every treatment to make sure the disease died and they didn’t. There's an element of desperation in that.

That’s not so different from what I was doing. In my early teens I started dealing with disordered eating. Then came anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation, and eventually psychosis, until I was diagnosed with bipolar disorder.

You could see my years of counselling as a reliance on therapy. Or you could see me as someone in a lot of pain looking for answers, trying to build a life that felt worth living. Or, the worst-case scenario, I had a remarkable streak of bad luck choosing incompetent health professionals.

I spent a little over 20 years moving out of denial, accepting the diagnosis, finding the right meds, learning self-management strategies, and doing deep trauma healing.

Eventually there came a time after years of those appointments when I moved from surviving to thriving. That didn't mean I stopped going to counselling—not yet. It meant I needed a maintenance program to help me stay well. Sort of like when you’ve reached your goal weight.

I've been on a maintenance program for the past 20 years and counting. For the last four years, I’ve seen my current therapist on an as-needed basis.

Of the 14 therapists I've seen, four were couples counsellors, including the sex therapist. My husband and I saw him twice. Sex therapy is uncomfortable. What a surprise.

Even when my husband and I were in couples therapy, I was still doing individual counselling. You can't say I'm commitment-phobic.

In my one-to-one therapy, I was not only learning tools to keep me mentally well, I was also trying to decide whether to leave my marriage.

My mental health was strong, even during this difficult time. So strong, in fact, that—with the help of 14 counsellors over 41 years of therapy—I was able to gather the courage to do one of the hardest things I've ever done: walk away from my 20-year relationship.

41 years may sound like dependency. But, for me, therapy helped set me free.
